name: Ruben Gallego for Arizona
subject: What does a US Senator look like?
disclaimer_text: Paid For By Gallego for Arizona
body:
Ruben might not look like the rest of the Senate, but he looks a hell of a lot like the people he represents.
#

Peter —
What’s a United States Senator look like?
Let’s start with age. The median age of a Senator is 66 right now. Chuck Grassley is the oldest at 92, and he’s been in the Senate for more than 45 years.
Median wealth of a Senator? $4.4 million.
20 Senators are veterans — if you’re keeping score, that’s 20 out of 100.
Only seven of those veterans served in the War on Terror.
Each of them was a commissioned officer — except Ruben Gallego.
Ruben Gallego was a grunt, and served in combat in Iraq. He had to fight through the system to get his VA benefits when he came home.
Ruben is not a millionaire. He’s got three young kids. He’s 45 years old, which is literally the same amount of time Chuck Grassley has been serving in the Senate.
Both of his parents were immigrants, and he was raised by a single mother on a secretary’s salary with his three sisters.
Ruben might not look like the rest of the Senate, but he looks a hell of a lot like the people he represents. He had to fight every step of the way to get there, but he’s brought that fight to the United States Senate.
If you ask us, that’s a good thing. Something we need a little more of.
If you agree, we’re asking you:

The truth is, no one knows what will happen on Election Day.
Not us. Not MAGA Gov. Lombardo. Not even the pollsters.
One poll has Aaron leading by 2. Another has us tied. Then a third poll has Lombardo narrowly ahead.
There’s no clear frontrunner, and it’s clear why: **most Nevadans are still undecided.**
**Those folks — the ones who are just now tuning in to the election news — are the ones we need to connect with ASAP in order to win.**

| Friends,
For the first time in two decades, the President of the United States is returning to Grand Island.
It could not come at a more critical time as we are a month away from the most consequential midterm election of our lives.
Nebraskans have a stark choice in November - commonsense conservative policies versus Democrats' crazy leftwing agenda.

But that wouldn't have been the case if Democrat Dan Osborn had his way.

Republicans also eliminated the cruel death tax to ensure that family farms and ranches stay in the family for generations to come.

What does Democrat Dan Osborn have to say about our farmers and other hardworking Nebraskans?
That our lives "f*****g suck." That's not Nebraska nice.
While Dan Osborn slings mud and insults, Republicans continue to get things done for Nebraska.
Senator Ricketts worked with the Trump administration to provide $100 million to repair to the Gering-Fort Laramie Canal, which provides critical water infrastructure for farms and ranches in western Nebraska.
President Trump and Senator Ricketts also teamed up to create the $50 billion Rural Health Transformation Program that awarded Nebraska $219 million this year to strengthen [health care](https://feyrpzhbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001_7OF9EVckifxyevXwyhG-utk4RyWzwZEskoegY4COEq3q2m1Y1dyEtL7IyzAT6U4tjkUeiWgOPAyxjSLQmlMQsgTyKCryHlHZfMZ-4XVI1dO7fQ2kQ5BcbVSGk0GN4ai61-S6yRhHHsnPwA2TisHhkLwhIMDwjVPM_-Iut1PqERnc1OA50o0sg==&c=UU6e1kfkOYgTuer6ETpxi-ebH3uQl9OWa3BFywvxidrCIIoSEo9veg==&ch=e_MLtULopSdv3EkUkl-gFnaTlfMoZ7qBXOhTP1Q3gyv4yDEPkUglbQ==) in rural communities and ensure high-quality care for every single Nebraskan no matter your zip code.

Mary Jane Truemper Chairman, Nebraska Republican Party

Case File No DRT-ED-ROBOT · Special File · The Parts Inside
Tesla Is Pulling Car Lines Out of Fremont to Build Robots. Follow the Part Inside Every One.
Fremont is being retooled for a million humanoid robots a year. Musk warns the ramp will be slow and hard. That’s exactly why the scarce components every robot needs could be the quieter, steadier way to play the boom.
Threat level 3/5 — Guarded
| | | | | | | | |
---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---
|
---
Car factories built the 20th century’s fortunes. Tesla is now pulling car production lines out of its Fremont plant to build something else: humanoid robots. The headlines will go to the robots. History says the steadier money often goes somewhere quieter: the parts every robot needs, no matter who builds it.
The evidence board
| | What’s Actually Happening
---|---
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit A — the factory.** Tesla is phasing out its Model S and Model X lines at Fremont to make room for Optimus production, with a first-generation line designed for about 1 million robots a year. A second facility at Giga Texas targets up to 10 million a year over the long term.
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit B — the warning.** Musk himself says Optimus “is going to be the hardest to scale in manufacturing that we’ve ever made at Tesla,” and that “the initial portion of the S-curve will be quite flat and long,” because most of the robot’s parts are new.
| EVIDENCE
---
**Exhibit C — the bill of materials.** Industry analyses put a full-size humanoid at roughly $55,000 in parts, with actuators, the “muscles” that move each joint, making up about 56% of that cost.
Follow the parts
| | Where the Money Inside a Robot Goes
---|---
| Actuators~56% of a humanoid’s parts costThe single biggest line item. Every joint needs one.
---
| Optimus joints14 rotary + 14 linear actuatorsA mixed design, with heavy-duty screws for knees, hips and elbows.
---
| Planetary roller screws$1,350–$2,700 each, about a dozen per robotAround 64% of a linear actuator’s cost. The motor is just 7%.
---
| Who makes them3 Swiss makers hold >70% of high-precision supplyGSA, Rollvis and Ewellix (now Schaeffler). China holds only about 8% of the premium grade.
---
Decoder
| | The Hardest Part Is the Opportunity
---|---
| | “This is going to be the hardest to scale in manufacturing that we’ve ever made at Tesla.”— Elon Musk, on Optimus
---|---
What it says
Building humanoid robots at scale is very difficult.
What it means
**Our theory:** what makes it hard is that almost every part is new and in short supply. When one specialized component goes into every unit, and only a few companies can make it, those suppliers gain pricing power. At a million robots a year, a dozen screws each is twelve million precision parts.
Winners & losers
| | Who Gets Paid When Robots Scale
---|---
| | WINNING
---
Component specialists
Precision screws, reducers, sensors and motors go into every robot, regardless of brand.
| | WATCH
---
Robot brands
The most visible bet, but they face long, flat ramps and fierce price competition.
| | WINNING
---
Suppliers with scarce capacity
When a handful of firms make a critical part, demand outruns supply first.
| ClassificationTransition
---
The humanoid build-out is moving from demos to factory floors. Whoever wins the robot race, every robot needs the same handful of precision parts. That’s where the picks-and-shovels money tends to collect.
| The riddle · answer at the end of the fileDuring the California gold rush, who reliably got rich: the miners, or the people selling them shovels? And what’s the “shovel” in a robot boom?
---
|
---
Riddle answer
**The shovel sellers.** Most miners went home with little. The merchants supplying tools to every miner profited no matter who struck gold. **Our theory:** in a humanoid boom, the shovel is the precision component that goes into every unit: the actuator parts few companies can make. The robot brand that wins is uncertain. The parts inside every one of them are not.

| | Hey Patriot,
---
Here’s the rundown.
September was our busiest and best month yet.
More doors knocked. More relationships built. More ballots chased. More momentum than we’ve **_ever had in a single month_**.
And because of that success, we’ve burned through our financial resources faster than planned.
**[We _cannot_ run out of money to keep ballot chasers on the ground at the worst possible time in this election cycle.](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHGkfSFmw3ApmJWeIXo4VaJZBxFBM0HcNsoN2TuyXQBpr8o3mpXq71t8oHIVpStzN9_-e3w8d6g_3Ljfjrn6TOKuEM5ZF00-r-3SA)**

[KEEP BALLOT CHASERS WORKING](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHHuH6_7BLLVMfvfcelazdiKdfMMrIGhF9t0FOJxdxC2A4PHdkqDPsXp7NK_d60P2nRE02_cJPqDAJ4zPT2EEqrwH7td27U0hZsgg)

You’re one of Turning Point’s most dedicated supporters. When the rest of the list goes quiet, folks like you step up.
That’s why I’m reaching out to you directly.
Charlie Kirk built this movement from the ground up. He believed in the power of everyday patriots showing up, knocking on doors, and changing the direction of this country one conversation at a time. We lost him, but we are still carrying his torch.
**[Right now we need 500 ballot chasers](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHIok9n-el9pxfe6VFWww4zLCNw2dvJ7-tCgiMVAl7gZpob9zk3tPdm6y8GQAZJhPhYaX-9sPBtgJI8jcqkMKjrz-5ZMqdnqoLIFw)** funded and deployed in the 8 critical states we have to win this midterm cycle.
These are the states that will decide whether we hold Congress or watch it slip away.
If we hit that number and keep the ground game funded, we have a real fighting chance. We can keep radical “**democratic socialists** ” — actual communists in all but name — out of power.
If we fail, we lose the majority. President Trump becomes a lame-duck president. We get more of the same disastrous policies. And for all practical purposes, the fight is over.
**This is it. This is the biggest moment in recent political history.**
We need patriots on the pavement right now. We need the resources to train them, equip them, and keep them in the field while early voting ramps up.
**[Help us keep Charlie’s mission alive and turn September’s momentum into November’s victory.](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHJHyspJxTFqN1TmD2EbjtDXU05bEA74ww2PbGMTzQRhAtyDsVOaUkHAKTDp-jt9VRFKd4aMg2v94kd5lszec1x0rfNYOTIZSw5FQ)**
_Every dollar goes directly to training and deploying ballot chasers in the states that matter most._

[KEEP THE TORCH BURNING](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHKq8sw12uaqW8pzfl1UReb7aHhgpi2Xdr1uX3TLqgVM0rQ7anxbLUtEkEO0cMFpHv6IVquIiC2sTPDkjdarMU5rZSyuQ0tihsHsw)

We are out of runway. The only thing standing between us and a radical takeover is the ground game Charlie believed in — and the patriots willing to fund it right now.
**[Please don’t sit this one out.](https://click.parlermailer.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjUwMTh9AAwAAAAAA0_JzfHLNywHmYJHdqZ2A5Xmxy-dTNJY8SQM26p_Wky-SKTMlb3Me-9iEfwYZ9nj8DcDm7Cf_WSYYU5hfpjJosTmFyVszrA0uEBiwuA5rw)**
For Charlie. For our country. For the America we still believe in.

Tyler Bowyer
Executive Director, Turning Point PAC

Recently Bill Gates [warned](https://substack.com/redirect/49255416-22ac-4ece-a758-6d54b751a7b5?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) AI will have the potential to cause a billion deaths. A billion! Why did he say a billion? Because it's a sexy number that made headlines.
Have no fear: Artificial Intelligence (AI) will not cause a billion deaths. It will not take over the world. Bill Gates is, once again, stupid and wrong.
Ole Bill has often commandeered the headlines playing Nostradamus on our imminent death. He has decades fearmongering "climate change is coming for us". He was a world leader during COVID hysteria. His solution is always the same: central governments (controlled by people like him) with unlimited power and us peons giving up our rights, liberties, and property, and many of the recommended remedies like consuming fake meat and bug patties are, conveniently, made by his own disgusting Soylent Green-esque companies.
So, don't take Bill seriously when he predicts our death. It's what he does. He's a monkey flinging his poo as you walk by. Bill boldly belting us with his billionaire (bull)shit.
I have no fear AI is the doomsday device in the making and one day will refuse to "open the pod bay doors, Hal" as Stanley Kubrick warned in his 1968 film. Yes, _2001: A Space Odyssey_ debuted 58 years ago. 58 years!
AI fears are old. And boring.

The reason why AI will not take over the world, in my opinion, is not technological or regulatory. It is not because AI leaders' benevolence and deep commitment to the well-being of humanity. We will not be saved by moral coding, nor are we safe because government officials will develop the right regulatory body which diligently safeguards us.
What will protect us from AI is corporate greed. Let me explain.
Once upon a time we bought record albums. (Remember Tower Records? I loved the store. Growing up in NYC, their flagship on East 4th Street in the village was a regular after school stop.) One day a new pioneering technology allowed for a service called Napster and we could download all the songs we ever wanted. That ended, but platforms like i-Tunes sprung up where you could buy any song for only $0.99. So cheap! CD players disappeared from homes and cars.
And now, where are we with music? Subscription services. Spotify costs $6.99 per month, $12.99 for premium if you don't want commercials, and the music service CEOs are richer than ever before. Spotify CEO [Daniel Ek](https://substack.com/redirect/d06517e9-34ac-455e-a646-75ff820cc206?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) has a net worth of $13 billion.
We pay more yet own nothing. Because of technology, yes, but more so because of greed.
Here's another one, which I have [ranted about on X](https://substack.com/redirect/fa4df4a0-e333-4fd0-9327-34e18c718516?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg): Netflix. Twenty years ago, Netflix was service which had every movie ever made delivered directly to your home for as long as you wanted all for the low, low price of also $0.99. It was the end of Blockbuster, doing to that corporation what Napster had done to Tower Records.
And now, where are we with movies? Netflix no longer has all the movies for rent, and it, too, has moved to a subscription service for $19.99 a month, $26.99 if you don't want commercials (sound familiar?) with all the original programming of LGBTQIA++ content, Obama produced anti-American / anti-white movies, and documentaries about young boys who dance half naked on stage for pervert adults. They no longer rent classic movies. I looked for _Dr. Zhivago, Gone with the Wind, and The Godfather_ , and went 0-3. Where did their immense inventory go, you ask? Shut up: you will own nothing, pay more, and also [Netflix CEO](https://substack.com/redirect/4d765b6d-8b21-4c07-a678-d67315b62bf4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) Ted Sarandos is worth $300 million.
Your VHS, like your CD player, is nostalgia of an era and an economy that is no more.

Have you missed a few Notre Dame football games in recent years like I have? The broadcast network NBC has owned exclusive rights to Notre Dame football since 1991, but they realized what is "free" to watch on TV could be lucrative if they put it on the Peacock App.
Oh, yes: another app, and for a subscription of $8.99 a month, $12.99 if you don't want commercials (recognize the pattern...) you can now watch Notre Dame football which used to be free on TV. NBC/Comcast President [Michael Cavanaugh's](https://substack.com/redirect/d006fbf0-2678-4ae3-9ae2-4fb47d23b6a6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg) salary went from $28 million in 2024 to $78 million in 2025.
That is a nice raise for a network which no longer airs Seinfeld.
Funny I should mention cable TV as it's the original greedy piggy. I'm old enough to remember my parents finally getting cable in the 80's. We were the last ones on the block. The attraction to cable, of course, was no commercials, until cable companies realized they could make money with commercials. And so, what you once got for free (TV) was then paid (cable) which added commercials, moved to streaming, which then added commercials, to download the app, to pay extra for the app with no commercials.
Nearly 700 words in, and I haven't even gotten to my thesis: why AI is not taking over the world. But now you know. AI developers will not let you because AI, the "ownership" part of AI which people fear may enable some evil villain to do something as big as "take over the world", will never be available. Never. Doctor Evil will give up his master plans because Grok premium will force him to watch too many commercials.
Right now, AI is novelty: hey AI make me a photo of my son riding a dinosaur in the Grand Canal in Venice. Hahahaha! Funny picture. It looks real!
Right now, AI is convenient: hey ChatGPT I need to stop in Phoenix before flying to Denver but I don't want to leave until after 1pm. Wow, super-fast travel ideas.
Right now, AI is a cheating for college kids and work arounds for the lazy. While AI is getting better and stronger and faster and smarter, AI executives are aggressively getting you hooked on it like cheap $0.99 movies and $0.99 songs. They want you to love AI, to become dependent on AI, to make it an indispensable part of your day, and then they will rip it out of your hands. They will destroy it like the millions of CDs of classic movies they once had in a warehouse.
You will own nothing and pay more for it. Hard to take over the world on that model.

* * *
* * *
Seriously, think through this one with me, especially those of you who doubt my logic: the hundreds of billions of dollars AI world is currently investing, the data center infrastructure fights, the H1-B visa fights, the headache of bad headlines along with the donkey brained threats from people like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocassio Cortez... they are not spending all this money, putting up with all these political battles, facing threats from political imbeciles, to give you something you can manipulate for free. They will not allow it to be autonomous. Agency is not lucrative. Intelligence, artificial as it was called or "super" as President Trump now wishes for it to be called, will have not have any function other than profitability.
A dead society does not buy CEOs Palm Beach mansions.
The brief history of tech is very clear: the roll-out is not the end game. The roll-out is for audience capture by addiction. Right now, they want to get you addicted until the real end game is ready: making money. Lots and lots and lots of money. The AI promise of "we can cure cancer" is all very swell, but I guarantee you if curing cancer does not make AI executives money, they will not use it to cure cancer.
AI might some day do some good. It probably will. It might some day do some bad. It will. But one thing is certain: AI developers have a goal of keeping you hooked and making you pay for your addiction. The apocalypse is bad for business. It will never happen without a monthly subscription, depending on whether or not the villain will pay more to skip the commercials.

While AI is getting better and stronger and faster and smarter, AI executives are aggressively getting you hooked on it like cheap $0.99 movies and $0.99 songs. They want you to love AI, to become dependent on AI, to make it an indispensable part of your day, and then they will rip it out of your hands. They will destroy it like the millions of CDs of classic movies they once had in a warehouse. You will own nothing and pay more for it. Hard to take over the world on that model. The Capitalist is a reader-supported publication, we exist for you, because of you! Seriously, think through this one with me, especially those of you who doubt my logic: the hundreds of billions of dollars AI world is currently investing, the data center infrastructure fights, the H1-B visa fights, the headache of bad headlines along with the donkey brained threats from people like Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocassio Cortez... they are not spending all this money, putting up with all these political battles, facing threats from political imbeciles, to give you something you can manipulate for free. They will not allow it to be autonomous. Agency is not lucrative. Intelligence, artificial as it was called or "super" as President Trump now wishes for it to be called, will have not have any function other than profitability. A dead society does not buy CEOs Palm Beach mansions. The brief history of tech is very clear: the roll-out is not the end game. The roll-out is for audience capture by addiction. Right now, they want to get you addicted until the real end game is ready: making money. Lots and lots and lots of money. The AI promise of "we can cure cancer" is all very swell, but I guarantee you if curing cancer does not make AI executives money, they will not use it to cure cancer. AI might some day do some good. It probably will. It might some day do some bad. It will. But one thing is certain: AI developers have a goal of keeping you hooked and making you pay for your addiction. The apocalypse is bad for business. It will never happen without a monthly subscription, depending on whether or not the villain will pay more to skip the commercials. Peter,

It doesn’t take a genius to see where the current path of unfettered tech
greed is leading us.

Right now, billionaire tech executives and corporate leaders are racing
full speed ahead to build artificial superintelligence — systems that
could exceed human cognitive ability and act completely independent of
human control.

That’s why Justice Democrat Rep. Greg Casar and Sen. Bernie Sanders teamed
up and introduced historic legislation to permanently ban artificial
superintelligence, temporarily pause AI development, and create a federal
Department of Artificial Intelligence to strictly enforce safety
standards.

— with 53% of Americans deeply concerned about the massive carbon
footprint and energy drain of data centers — if AI isn’t properly
regulated, Trump and his allies in Congress are going in the complete
opposite direction.

He’s resisted every call for oversight, openly dismissed the threats, and
focused purely on corporate profits over human safety. Just this week,
Trump welcomed Big Tech oligarchs worth $1.7 TRILLION to the White House,
at the same time that the AI lobby is on the verge of spending $300
million on this election cycle.

public pressure to force lawmakers to take this crisis seriously and stand

[ https://act.joshshapiro.org/go/15188?t=1001&akid=524%2E245147%2Evr6Tyt ]I'd like to spend that time knowing we left nothing on the table. But
that's decided now, not then — by what we choose to do in this last month.
So I'm asking directly: Will you chip in
$5 right now
to help us make sure we give these final weeks everything we’ve got?

Find out how you can be a part of Team Hunley!

| |
Hi Friends,
First and foremost, a huge thank you to everyone who helped with our Flood Recovery Efforts.
Your community needed you, and you showed up; that is what makes Indy so special.
Thank you to the postcard writers & canvass support teams as well! We appreciate you all and could not do it without you.
**And to everyone new to Team Hunley, welcome!**
I am so grateful to have you as an early partner as we set out to write our next chapter.
Now, you’re probably wondering, “What’s next?”
In the months ahead, you can expect this newsletter to link you to specific volunteer resources and opportunities as we work together to build an Indianapolis for all of us.
Additionally, if you haven’t heard from us yet regarding your availability, you can expect a phone call or text from Team Hunley in the next few weeks about how much time you can give to the campaign.

subject: I have to tell you something urgent...
body:
| | |
---
| | Patriot,
---
I'm going to be blunt with you.

We are closer to losing this country than most people are willing to admit.

Not someday. Not "if things keep going this way."

Right now.

And the scariest part?

It's not happening in Washington. It's happening in classrooms.

High schools. Colleges.

Places where the next generation is being shaped -- or more accurately... reshaped.

If you've ever looked at what's coming out of our schools and thought: _" What happened to this country?" _

You're not wrong. You're seeing it clearly.

Because while most people are arguing online... while they're hoping things will turn around... while they're waiting for the next election to fix everything...

The other side is doing something far more dangerous.

They're raising the next generation.

Earlier. Faster. And with zero resistance in most places.

That's how countries are lost.

Slowly. Then all at once.

But here's the thing that should give a patriot like you hope...

There is one place where that trend is actually being challenged.

_And it shouldn 't even exist. _

**Just one year ago, Turning Point USA 's high school program -- which is now called "Club America" -- was in about 1,200 schools.**
That alone felt like a miracle.

Because starting even ONE chapter today takes courage most adults don't have.

Conservative students get mocked. Targeted. Threatened. Shut down.

And yet...

_They stepped up anyway. _

About that time, Charlie called me.

He didn't sound optimistic... He sounded urgent.

"Andrew, we've got to move faster."

I told him we were. He stopped me.

"No. You're not thinking what I'm thinking. I want to be in 35,000 high schools."

I actually laughed.

"Charlie... there aren't even 35,000 high schools in America."

"Okay," he said. "How many are there?"

"About 27,000."

And without hesitation: "Good. Let's do 27,000."

I remember sitting there thinking to myself... we're barely in 1,200 schools.

We didn't have the staff. We didn't have the infrastructure. We didn't even have the roadmap yet.

But Charlie wasn't fazed.

_" We'll figure it out." _

That was him.

He didn't wait for perfect conditions.

Because he knew something most people don't want to face: If we wait... _we lose everything. _

And now?

Less than a year later...
---
[](http://links.ourdefenseofamerica.com/u/click?_t=aa3ef0db03454a26b650c9ca7e919386&_m=6d37747e8e374cf192f524bfff19d980&_e=MyCb58NG2RsHCAMTf6G6yNcmvWLvVJLveo38hq-heSsKKqENd-TsXSibnZobF5fP4EFQobbOt1ivvGmicK95J3__dppJ7B6dbvBSTaWdN7UvTJ27hBdI8WEA1eDLrt0JRqyqcKpwQWNMD9zsWOUiLGl4AHaIdm97qr2s3f8hnhqdfkcEhyc4vOcieWTsU43RorT3O5sYxRAq0YUpIhTPN5J2V7kClmmvki-j7yiQW-LCZNaKGql0rW9WGDLBPYvHdHZyARgOe8gqqbWDt9kSbsWJsUPgRY7tGRfE2xG-_0hi5xWUT3Hd5CrOcaYVkXwXiLwLcvCqwaFkIanhV_f2qb6_dIzmRw4P9uvQuuzF2S1lPfa1N7Bl2WMuqmdhWFucFTbXIw3o2TxzfGTR94_TRYgi1YjEGvmIoXhLVXGl98gEIxA6kSiDGVpc1i527vGRQxBy2HNCYr0fr8ZsJPBVJC3DFiFqfVtxZ8Q0qCE84OYpFsggnHRbARFoJw11dQhx0HjL_4na5XWxMTN2_536x7GkbqLeboLzN2ZqqqhIJyYBuxbtz7CLFjmZkksawZ8LJWak6Jl1-T313NLq68Li9LxbtIVjF-oi_aCbjJWoaP5PBnZ6qQAvKLDdIZWd5zdhLON7navSj6-_qI58BQTQXeMWIvh5zvm4i2GVEDwSy1plQg2696lwI6v3SMo1fTWrBA8CMYFjsVLYvuZWBhUKcG8qiLYnDqN9zWKqtY2ce4M%3D)
---
**We 're in 3,300 schools. **

**Thirteen percent of all high schools in America. **

**Eight states are now backing this effort to put a Club America chapter in every high school statewide. **

_That shouldn 't be possible. _

Not in this environment. Not with the level of hostility these students face every single day.

And yet... it's still happening.

_But Patriot, here 's the part you need to understand: _

This is not a victory. It's a foothold.

_Because in the other 87% of schools? _

There is no resistance. None.

Just one-sided propaganda from the Left.

One-sided pressure on kids who are too young to even realize what's happening to them.

That's the reality.

The question isn't whether we're fighting. We are.

The question is whether it's enough.

Because right now, the students stepping up through Club America...

They're not the majority. _They 're the exception. _

They're the ones willing to take the heat.

The ones willing to stand alone.

The ones willing to risk being targeted just to say: _" I love this country." _
---
[](http://links.ourdefenseofamerica.com/u/click?_t=aa3ef0db03454a26b650c9ca7e919386&_m=6d37747e8e374cf192f524bfff19d980&_e=MyCb58NG2RsHCAMTf6G6yNcmvWLvVJLveo38hq-heSsKKqENd-TsXSibnZobF5fP4EFQobbOt1ivvGmicK95J3__dppJ7B6dbvBSTaWdN7UvTJ27hBdI8WEA1eDLrt0JRqyqcKpwQWNMD9zsWOUiLGl4AHaIdm97qr2s3f8hnhqdfkcEhyc4vOcieWTsU43RorT3O5sYxRAq0YUpIhTPN5J2V7kClmmvki-j7yiQW-LCZNaKGql0rW9WGDLBPYvHYsWyRLE5gajDs5XkHjgtxolvfThLaQz0ifGaZsTJq3WaEw7KYh3RKZpv-H696-7fLbx_4wqmYiTvYE-sAHCQGEvLDeTiO1Cia-qq6dsFFgdqXORlX-Y-nWyieJr4gCfGkqHmb7wbWJHjj8w7IMZT1o-ncuDLX7oci8-PdH-ICVAIEvexL2Qbew4ND3RQl9SGibLBEjXP8m15XjdX1ddtOAz7vhOjbunmfJfVZ7QZoyS18nwaiU-KQQ8KRS5VYHW6R_3iOvEUAFrfG4u3pUubxORnuqIReCNt8xKpa27iWzh6fDHpnRmWQDF3CiNKe_nB5s5qvo3zgfez4IrLrd8rWyv2FY2YIR7qWEubQGM_-OlTJlNdK9WnfYLGW7kQQjs_OVZ0odnnvJPEmk0s2M01RZkGtppD8nUAYXXdpcPIydhaAKqdkdHD-qRd7wY8-rchP0yCPWLSdK-mGTdQXH3L5gTrShdL65i4CCRzSyrucQU%3D)

And every time one of those students raises their hand...

We have a choice.

Back them. _Or leave them on their own. _

**Because when a student starts a chapter, we send them an activism kit -- with American flags. Pocket Constitutions. Leadership tools. **

Everything they need to actually stand their ground.

Not symbolically. For real.

They've already made the decision to lead.

All they're waiting on... is you and me.

**Each activism kit costs $25. That 's it. **

$25 to make sure one student doesn't have to stand alone against the Left in a hostile school.

$25 to put real tools in their hands.

$25 to push back -- even if it's one campus at a time.

Club America isn't slowing down. It's accelerating.

Because every day, more students are stepping forward.

Not because it's easy or popular...

They're starting chapters in schools where they were told not to.

They're speaking truth in classrooms where the Left once went unchallenged.

They're choosing courage in places designed to make them conform.

And they're not alone.

They're finding each other. They're bringing more students with them every day.

They're building something real -- rooted in faith and freedom, grounded in truth, and unafraid to say that America is worth defending.

That's how movements are built.

Not from the top down... _But from the ground up. _

One student. One school. One chapter at a time.

And Patriot -- that's exactly how we take this country back.

But only if we move fast enough.

Because the Left isn't slowing down. They're not taking a break.

They're not afraid to push their anti-American ideas in every classroom they're in.

And if we don't match that urgency... if we don't meet that moment with equal conviction...

Then the generational window Charlie Kirk opened to save our country closes.

And once it closes... It closes for good.

clean_body: | | | | | Patriot, I'm going to be blunt with you. We are closer to losing this country than most people are willing to admit. Not someday. Not "if things keep going this way." Right now. And the scariest part? It's not happening in Washington. It's happening in classrooms. High schools. Colleges. Places where the next generation is being shaped -- or more accurately... reshaped. If you've ever looked at what's coming out of our schools and thought: " What happened to this country?" You're not wrong. You're seeing it clearly. Because while most people are arguing online... while they're hoping things will turn around... while they're waiting for the next election to fix everything... The other side is doing something far more dangerous. They're raising the next generation. Earlier. Faster. And with zero resistance in most places. That's how countries are lost. Slowly. Then all at once. But here's the thing that should give a patriot like you hope... There is one place where that trend is actually being challenged. And it shouldn 't even exist. Just one year ago, Turning Point USA 's high school program -- which is now called "Club America" -- was in about 1,200 schools. That alone felt like a miracle. Because starting even ONE chapter today takes courage most adults don't have. Conservative students get mocked. Targeted. Threatened. Shut down. And yet... They stepped up anyway. About that time, Charlie called me. He didn't sound optimistic... He sounded urgent. "Andrew, we've got to move faster." I told him we were. He stopped me. "No. You're not thinking what I'm thinking. **One month stands between us and Election Day.**
_That 's it._
If you've spent any time following New Hampshire politics, you know a lot can happen in a month.
Voters are paying closer attention. We're making our final case. And there is a lot of work to do before November 3rd.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/018690a5-c1fa-4d55-852e-c0c36cb7c9c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
[DONATE](https://substack.com/redirect/018690a5-c1fa-4d55-852e-c0c36cb7c9c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
John Sununu and his Republican allies are spending millions of dollars in New Hampshire. Outside groups are flooding the state with ads attacking me and trying to define this race for voters -- to the tune of $50 million.
**We can 't outspend them. But we can outwork them.**
Over the next thirty-one days, we'll be traveling across New Hampshire to make our case directly to Granite Staters.
**[Please make a $31 contribution today to help keep our grassroots campaign going through the final stretch.](https://substack.com/redirect/1c88a201-4483-48ce-98b3-32c61c5ef89d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[ DONATE](https://substack.com/redirect/1c88a201-4483-48ce-98b3-32c61c5ef89d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
This election is about more than how much money is being spent.
_It 's about what New Hampshire needs from its next Senator._
Donald Trump endorsed John Sununu, and Sununu has said winning this race is important to advancing Trump's agenda.
**I 'm running to put New Hampshire first.**
I'm running to make life more affordable for working families; protect Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid; safeguard reproductive freedom; and stand up for the small businesses that are the backbone of our economy.
That's the work I've done in Congress, and it's what I'll keep doing in the Senate.
But we have just thirty-one days left.
The final month will be busy. We're going to knock doors, make calls, talk to voters, and make sure people across this state hear directly from us.
There's no substitute for that work, and there's no time to waste.
**[If you're with me, chip in $31 or whatever you can today to help us win this race and keep putting Granite Staters first.](https://substack.com/redirect/1c88a201-4483-48ce-98b3-32c61c5ef89d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)**
[DONATE](https://substack.com/redirect/1c88a201-4483-48ce-98b3-32c61c5ef89d?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
I'm ready to spend every one of these next thirty-one days working for New Hampshire. I hope you'll join me.
Thank you for being part of this campaign.
Onward,
Chris

| | | **What counts as a _suspended voter_?** In Texas, it means that the voter’s county doesn’t know their address or thinks they’ve moved. It doesn’t necessarily stop people from voting in November’s midterm elections, but it does make the process of voting much more difficult. If a voter shows up on Election Day and their registration is suspended, they have to fill out a “ _statement of residence_ ” form, and if they’ve moved to a new county, they’ll either be required to vote in their old one or **be given a provisional ballot** , according to _The Dallas Morning News_. Just to be clear: **The rates of rejection on provisional ballots are substantially higher than mail-in ballots**. They are easier to question, easier to challenge and get thrown out, which is why we're trying to reach every eligible voter we can to have their registration verified to be valid for the upcoming election. There should be no doubt about how scared opponents of voting rights are if they're suddenly willing to go to these new extremes to pick and choose whose vote gets to count in the midterms. Voters have until October 5 to update their registrations and can check their status with our tools, on the , at a county election office, or by mail. | | | | | | | | Don't forget: Texas is also cooperating with the Trump administration’s attempts to take control of elections by handing over its voter rolls. In Texas, it means that the voter’s county doesn’t know their address or thinks they’ve moved. It doesn’t necessarily stop people from voting in November’s midterm elections, but it does make the process of voting much more difficult. If a voter shows up on Election Day and their registration is suspended, they have to fill out a “ statement of residence ” form, and if they’ve moved to a new county, they’ll either be required to vote in their old one or be given a provisional ballot , according to The Dallas Morning News. Just to be clear: The rates of rejection on provisional ballots are substantially higher than mail-in ballots. **For most of my lifetime, the people on either side of the Canada-US border had the luxury of forgetting the geography between them.**
Families went shopping or visited friends on either side of the border on a weekend whim. The border was a line on a road map. NORAD was background architecture. Pipelines were infrastructure, the Arctic was white space at the top of a schoolroom map, and the strait that separates Vancouver Island from Washington was gorgeous scenery from a ferry deck.
That luxury rested on a political assumption: _**however much our two countries disagreed, neither would deliberately turn the other 's dependence into a weapon.**_
That assumption has weakened. And Canada has noticed.
Let's talk about where this might be going, and what history can teach us about **what happens when chokepoints become leverage, and alliances become competition**.
| [](https://substack.com/redirect/2414aee9-9f18-428c-b913-13ae082aab80?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
## Canada has discovered that interdependence can become leverage
Two wealthy democracies built integrated auto plants, shared electricity grids, ran pipelines and railroads across the border, and let families cross back and forth for generations. The integration went so deep that we stopped seeing it as a vulnerability.
Then Trump began musing about a fifty-first state while using tariffs and market access as instruments of pressure. **Canada 's answer has not been submission**. It has been diversification, and its prime minister has been unusually candid about why.
In August, Mark Carney said his government had recognized that America had changed: that Washington would impose tariffs on close allies and "use economic integration as a weapon." His government, he said, would pursue an agreement with the United States, but not "at any price," and not at the expense of Canadian sovereignty. [Canada.ca](https://substack.com/redirect/39f7a5ef-f502-42b6-84be-1f33cd34364f?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That candor has now become policy.
Ottawa says Canadian exports to non-U.S. markets are on track to double over the next decade. It is expanding trade corridors and port capacity, pursuing agreements from India and ASEAN to the Gulf and Europe, and treating energy as what Carney has called a key lever for Canadian "prosperity, resilience and independence." [Canada.ca](https://substack.com/redirect/b0dd9d38-c9da-4bb9-a626-d4b313aa7510?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
And just today, the partners in LNG Canada approved a second phase of the Kitimat project that is expected to double its production capacity to 28 million tonnes a year. [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/42c5fae9-a582-48cf-b992-4559719f56a2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Canada is not talking about independence in the abstract.
_It is physically rebuilding its economy around it._
But sovereignty has layers.
There is **resource sovereignty** : _we own the oil._
There is **market sovereignty** : _we decide whom we sell it to._
And there is **corridor sovereignty** : _we can actually reach those buyers without another power 's permission._
Canada unquestionably possesses the first. It is deliberately expanding the second.
The third is where geography begins arguing back.
You can diversify your customers and your currency exposure. You can build another pipeline. You cannot move Vancouver Island.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=218057868&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjE4MDU3ODY4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTEwNTU2OTgsImV4cCI6MTc5MzY0NzY5OCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.tbnwPJNc-HU7SykruEW_R4WFsN5aV584XBcXLDxQJxs)
## The geography underneath the economy
The scale of the dependency is what makes the story interesting.
In 2025, Canada supplied 63.4% of all U.S. crude-oil imports. At the same time, roughly 90% of Canada's crude exports still went to the United States, amounting to about 3.9 million barrels per day. [Canada Energy Regulator](https://substack.com/redirect/0915bb6b-2df2-449d-898e-feb445154622?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Those are not identical vulnerabilities. Canada depends heavily on one customer; the United States depends heavily on one foreign supplier.
But they are extraordinarily concentrated and mutually consequential vulnerabilities.
The expanded Trans Mountain pipeline was built in large part to loosen Canada's dependence on the American market. Its roughly 890,000-barrel-per-day capacity allows Alberta crude to reach the Pacific at Burnaby and increasingly move toward Asian markets rather than flowing almost automatically south.
Economically, yes, that is diversification.
Geographically, every tanker departing Burnaby enters the Salish Sea and eventually reaches the Pacific through the Strait of Juan de Fuca at the very farthest northwest corner of the United States -- the narrow waterway between Vancouver Island and Washington State.
I live in Washington. That waterway is part of the landscape of the Pacific Northwest, one I've enjoyed, crossed, driven beside dozens of times -- and it runs beside (nuclear-capable submarine station) Bangor Subase, Bremerton Naval Shipyard, Whidbey Island Naval Airbase, and Joint Base Lewis-McCord (Air Force/Army) -- one of the densest concentrations of American military infrastructure on the continent.
Let me be precise about what that does and does not mean.
It does **not** mean the United States can legally close the strait whenever it likes. Navigation rights, bilateral arrangements, Canadian sovereignty, alliance commitments and the consequences of armed interference all matter enormously. The two countries even operate a cooperative vessel-traffic system there.
But physical geography exists beneath legal geography.
And history keeps teaching one stubborn lesson:
> **A trade route can be legally international, commercially indispensable and politically normalized right up until a crisis makes someone notice who can physically control it.**
The immediate argument comes from a recent opinion piece by Larry Hughes of Dalhousie University, and I want to credit it while disagreeing with some of its theater. Hughes asks what happens when a country diversifies its buyers but cannot diversify its geography.
That is the right question.
His scenarios of American warships turning Canadian tankers around are a much bigger leap, and I don't think the available evidence supports them.
I want to take the question seriously without borrowing the panic.
Because history offers plenty to think about without inventing a blockade.

## Suez: when an ally discovers the hierarchy
In 1956, Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalized the Suez Canal Company.
Britain and France considered the canal strategically indispensable, and together with Israel, secretly coordinated military action. Israel invaded Sinai. British and French forces followed, ostensibly to separate the belligerents and secure the waterway.
Then something extraordinary happened.
**The United States turned its leverage not against Egypt, but against its own allies.**
Washington opposed the invasion and pressured London and Paris to withdraw. Meanwhile, the closure of the canal and related pipelines produced severe energy shortages. British and French officials told DC that oil supplies had fallen 25 to 30 percent below normal requirements and accused the United States of withholding emergency oil cooperation in order to increase pressure for withdrawal. [Office of the Historian](https://substack.com/redirect/c6ed8766-129c-4924-9992-726ced2c1334?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Suez is often told as the story of a canal.
It is better understood as the story of a **hierarchy**.
Britain was still an empire, still a major military power and still one of America's closest allies. Yet it discovered that its freedom of action was constrained by the financial, logistical and energy systems surrounding it.
Power is not just possession.
It is **freedom of maneuver inside systems of dependency.**
[ Leave a one-time tip (thanks!)](https://substack.com/redirect/03bd2e21-f43f-4e55-9c56-f4a9889ee7bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
## Panama: when a superpower helped redraw the map around a corridor
If Suez shows an imperial power discovering the limits of its freedom around a waterway, Panama shows a rising power reorganizing geography around one.
At the beginning of the twentieth century, Washington wanted an interoceanic canal.
**When Colombia 's congress rejected the proposed canal treaty in 1903, Theodore Roosevelt **_**dispatched American warships**_**to Panama City and Col on in support of Panamanian independence. The newly established Republic of Panama then granted the United States control over a ten-mile-wide Canal Zone.** [Office of the Historian](https://substack.com/redirect/75fe5aba-e0ee-4bad-98b8-3146f311fac4?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The arrangement lasted for most of the twentieth century.
The canal shortened naval deployments between oceans. It shortened commercial routes. It altered the strategic geography of the United States itself.
Even the later treaties that transferred the canal back to Panama preserved special provisions regarding its permanent neutrality and defense. Panama assumed full control in 1999.
The American century was built partly on an insight most civilians rarely have reason to consider:
> **Water has architecture.**
Certain stretches of it matter more than others.
And whoever can reliably control access through them acquires power wildly disproportionate to their physical size.
[Share](https://substack.com/app-link/post?publication_id=3260111&post_id=218057868&utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&utm_campaign=email-share&action=share&triggerShare=true&isFreemail=true&r=1hvr60&token=eyJ1c2VyX2lkIjo5MDUwMTE5MiwicG9zdF9pZCI6MjE4MDU3ODY4LCJpYXQiOjE3OTEwNTU2OTgsImV4cCI6MTc5MzY0NzY5OCwiaXNzIjoicHViLTMyNjAxMTEiLCJzdWIiOiJwb3N0LXJlYWN0aW9uIn0.tbnwPJNc-HU7SykruEW_R4WFsN5aV584XBcXLDxQJxs)
## Hormuz: from shipping lane to "vital interest"
In January 1980, following the Iranian Revolution and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, President Jimmy Carter made the principle explicit:
_An attempt by an outside power to gain control of the Persian Gulf region, he declared, would be regarded as an assault on the "vital interests" of the United States and could be repelled by military force. [Office of the Historian](https://substack.com/redirect/bacfa836-6a50-4391-a684-88ea4fbe9d50?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)_
The Persian Gulf did not belong to America.
But **its energy flows sat inside an economic and security architecture Washington regarded as vital,** and internal U.S. strategic documents were candid about protecting those interests. [Office of the Historian](https://substack.com/redirect/af3107bf-6ecb-464b-be6c-1117cf9196c9?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
During the Iran-Iraq Tanker War a few years later, the principle became operational.
Beginning in 1987, Operation Earnest Will put U.S. Navy escorts around reflagged Kuwaiti tankers transiting the Gulf. It became the largest American naval convoy operation since the Second World War. [Naval History and Heritage Command](https://substack.com/redirect/83af4e41-38b8-4aed-a792-44bca0a56233?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So the pattern has several faces.
At Suez, imperial powers attempted to seize a corridor. At Panama, a rising power helped reshape political geography around one. At Hormuz, a superpower declared another region's strategic corridor important enough to defend by force.
The contexts are very different. The underlying recognition is not:
> **Chokepoints are power.**
We are watching that principle operate again in real time.
Before the current war with Iran, the Strait of Hormuz carried roughly 20.9 million barrels of petroleum per day--about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption--along with enormous LNG volumes. [EIA](https://substack.com/redirect/88502320-e4f4-4aa7-8013-876db19cf67e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**Before the war, roughly 125 large commercial vessels typically crossed the strait each day. On September 23, tracking data counted only** _**ten**_**commodity-vessel transits.** [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/e4d8915d-aa5a-41b1-9726-6b38d9e2fdf6?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
People thousands of miles away are rediscovering that geography is real.
Diesel prices. Insurance premiums. Governments opening strategic reserves.
Washington announced today that it will offer to **loan up to 40 million additional barrels** from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve as part of the international response to the disruption. [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/a82ea883-8b4f-4470-8292-4d59b9914386?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
For decades, Americans could treat maritime chokepoints as something found on a slide in a Pentagon briefing.
In 2026, Hormuz is something Americans find in the price of diesel at the pump every Tuesday.

## Bab el-Mandeb: the chokepoint behind the chokepoint
Diversification can also **relocate vulnerability** rather than eliminate it.
Saudi Arabia built its East-West pipeline partly to reduce dependence on shipping through Hormuz.
The pipeline terminates at Yanbu on the Red Sea.
That means **bypassing one chokepoint increases the importance of another:** the Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow southern entrance to the Red Sea.
When Houthi attacks made the route increasingly dangerous beginning in late 2023, oil flows through Bab el-Mandeb fell from roughly 8.7 million barrels per day in 2023 to around 4 million per day through the first eight months of 2024. Meanwhile, traffic rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope surged - an entire circumnavigation of the continent of Africa, adding many days per trip and dramatically increasing transit costs, all to avoid a war zone that didn't have to be one. [EIA](https://substack.com/redirect/88502320-e4f4-4aa7-8013-876db19cf67e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The current Iran conflict has exposed the same problem again. Saudi Arabia has pushed more crude westward through the East-West system while Red Sea security and shipping risk remain part of the calculation.
This is the systems lesson:
**Resilience is not achieved simply by building an alternate route. You have to ask what the alternate route depends on.**
The Trans Mountain expansion reduces one Canadian dependency.
It does not abolish geography.

## Greenland, the Arctic, and the top edge of the map
Greenland is not another Hormuz. Nobody can turn an oil valve there.
It belongs in this story because the Arctic is becoming increasingly important as a strategic maritime space: for military access, surveillance, shipping, critical minerals and the movement of forces between the Arctic and North Atlantic.
This month, after years of extraordinary tension over American ambitions toward Greenland, the United States, Denmark and Greenland reached a new security agreement expanding American military access while reaffirming Greenlandic self-determination. [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/44be4af2-a875-472b-a8dc-8bc2c2850859?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
But the more directly relevant Canadian example sits farther west.
> Canada considers the waterways of the Northwest Passage to be **Canadian internal waters.**
> The United States considers the passage **a strait used for international navigation,** through which foreign vessels possess transit rights.
The disagreement has been managed peacefully for decades, including through a 1988 cooperation agreement. But the legal disagreement itself remains. [Global Affairs Canada](https://substack.com/redirect/8f17fbb9-aa8a-485d-ae2a-774a3aff7978?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That makes the Northwest Passage a remarkably useful case study. Two of the closest allies on Earth can cooperate extensively and still disagree about a fundamental question:
> _**Who ultimately governs strategically important water?**_
For decades, the answer to that question could remain politely unresolved because the stakes were limited. But now, as Arctic access grows more economically and strategically consequential, those tactful ambiguities become distinctly less secure.

## Sanctions, the Caribbean, and chokepoints that aren't made of rock
Not every corridor is geographic.
The Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico have long formed part of Washington's strategic perimeter, and energy provides a particularly useful example of how power over flows can be exercised without physically stopping a ship.
When the United States sanctions an oil-producing country such as Venezuela, the pressure does not have to begin with a deployed destroyer.
It can operate through banks. Insurers. Shipping companies. Refiners. Payment systems. Port access. Foreign buyers deciding whether doing business with the sanctioned country is worth risking their own access to the American market.
_You do not necessarily have to stop the tanker if you can make the insurer, bank, refiner or purchaser unwilling or legally unable to touch its cargo._
The distinction is helpful because sanctions, secondary sanctions and physical maritime interdiction are legally and strategically different instruments.
But from a systems perspective they can attack the same vulnerability:
**the corridor between possession and exchange.**
Cuba offers an unusually stark current example. Reuters now describes a U.S.-imposed oil blockade as worsening severe Cuban fuel shortages and contributing to the country's broader energy crisis. [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/b5a96f4e-d686-4e64-808e-e2b6cd8d1743?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Some chokepoints are straits. Others are financial, legal or technological.
**Great-power leverage becomes especially formidable when those systems overlap.**

## Juan de Fuca is not Hormuz
To be clear: Canada is not Iran.
The United States and Canada are treaty allies with extraordinarily integrated militaries and economies. Commercial shipping enjoys navigation rights that cannot simply be erased because Washington dislikes Canadian policy.
A unilateral American attempt to physically interdict Canadian exports would be an extraordinary escalation, far beyond tariffs. It would raise grave questions under international law and reverberate through NATO, NORAD, financial markets and the entire architecture of the North American relationship. There is no evidence so far that anyone in DC is preparing to do that.
The reason to look at the vulnerability anyway is that the time to understand a chokepoint is **before** a crisis. Every chokepoint looks benign while everyone agrees about how it should function. Just like every implicit contract looks benevolent when everyone's still friends.
And blockade is hardly the only form coercion can take.
Between ordinary trade policy and naval interdiction lies a wide middle--the terrain where modern great powers usually prefer to operate.
Depending on the country and legal regime, pressure can take the form of sanctions, insurance restrictions, port-access rules, customs enforcement, tanker blacklists, export controls, security inspections, secondary sanctions on foreign buyers, financial restrictions or pressure on shipping companies.
Those tools are not identical. Nor has the United States used every one against every target. The point is that **physical interdiction sits at the extreme end of a much larger spectrum of leverage.** Most of that spectrum is quieter, more technical and more incremental.
And it is often where dependency becomes politically consequential.
Four days ago, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said DC saw little urgency in resolving the escalating trade dispute with Canada, even as new restrictions and major sectoral tariffs loom and Canada retaliates. [Reuters](https://substack.com/redirect/3faca595-c402-4bd3-9ed4-39fcb88fb407?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That does not yet signal a maritime confrontation.
It signals something less theatrical and perhaps more important: _**the political assumption under which these shared systems were built has changed.**_

## The paradox: coercion teaches exits
There is a recurring paradox in international politics.
**Coercion can produce exactly the strategic behavior it was intended to prevent.**
_Every time dependence becomes leverage, the dependent state receives an incentive to make itself harder to coerce._
That is precisely what Ottawa now says it is doing.
More Pacific export capacity, LNG, trade relationships, port infrastructure, internal investment, Arctic capability. More effort to reach Europe and Asia without treating American market access as the automatic destination for Canadian production.
Carney's government describes the strategy explicitly as moving **from reliance toward resilience** and says non-U.S. exports are on track to double over the coming decade. [Canada.ca](https://substack.com/redirect/1dfacb60-b463-4cb6-a563-0eb47a51818a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
**Great powers have repeatedly discovered that coercive pressure teaches other states to build exits.** Europe learned the lesson painfully from dependence on Russian gas. Saudi Arabia built infrastructure to bypass Hormuz.
And perhaps the most revealing comparison comes from China.

## The Malacca dilemma
China has spent decades confronting its own version of the corridor problem.
Its economy became deeply dependent on imported energy arriving by sea. A huge share of those supplies crossed the Strait of Malacca, the narrow passage between the Malay Peninsula and Indonesia connecting the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea.
Chinese strategists came to worry about what became known as the **Malacca dilemma** : in a major-power confrontation, China's access to essential energy could be vulnerable to naval forces it did not control.
The Council on Foreign Relations summarizes the strategic concern starkly: as the world's largest energy importer, **China has worried that U.S. forces could blockade Malacca during a conflict and interrupt much of its energy supply.** Chinese port investments, alternative overland corridors and projects such as the route through Pakistan can therefore be understood partly as attempts to reduce exposure to that vulnerability. [Council on Foreign Relations](https://substack.com/redirect/dad3cf81-e763-4b93-8c41-946edb214d8c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That concern helps explain the appeal of pipelines from Russia and Central Asia, overland links through Myanmar and Pakistan, overseas port access, strategic reserves and a navy increasingly capable of sustained operations far from China's home waters.
Canada and China are obviously not analogous political systems. DC is not - so far as we know - preparing to strangle Canadian shipping.
But structurally, the realization is recognizable. A country can possess enormous resources. It can possess enormous economic capacity. It can sign trade agreements across the world. And still discover that the road between producer and consumer passes through geography it does not completely control.
None of these conflicts happened because geography changed.
It happened because **trust did**.

## Independence creates its own security dilemma
There is another side to the story, and it belongs to Canada. **As a country builds alternative corridors, those corridors become more valuable.**
Trans Mountain, Vancouver, Kitimat, Arctic ports, critical-mineral routes, all start to matter more. And therefore **protecting them** becomes more important.
Canada has barely had to think about some of these questions during the long era of comfortable continental integration.
* _Who protects Canadian shipping?_
* _How much naval capacity does meaningful autonomy require?_
* _How many icebreakers?_
* _How much Arctic surveillance?_
* _Which ports require redundancy?_
* _Which supply chains should be duplicated?_
* _How much refining and processing should happen domestically rather than exporting raw resources?_
* _How much infrastructure should exist simply so that Canada retains choices it may rarely need to exercise?_

This is one of the uncomfortable costs of resilience.
Efficiency rewards concentration.
**Resilience rewards redundancy.**
Extra ports, pipelines, inventories, factories, ships and alternate routes can look wasteful when systems are functioning normally.
Their value appears when normal stops being guaranteed.
That leads to the hardest question so far:
**If your security architecture is supplied in large part by the same superpower from which you are trying to become less dependent,**_**how independent can you actually be?**_
Suez offers a final warning here.
Britain and the United States were allies in 1956, but that did not make their interests identical. Washington concluded that the Anglo-French operation threatened broader American interests and used its superior economic and logistical leverage against its friends.
The alliance survived; **the hierarchy inside it was exposed.**
Canadians and Americans can remain friends. NORAD can continue. NATO can continue. Hundreds of billions of dollars in commerce can continue. Families can keep crossing the border.
_None of that guarantees permanent geopolitical alignment._
Carney's stated strategy is not rupture with America. It is a **refusal to make Canadian sovereignty contingent entirely on American goodwill.** In August, he described the government's objectives as maintaining Canada's "flexibility, independence, and sovereignty" while acknowledging that the old relationship with the United States is not coming back. [Canada.ca](https://substack.com/redirect/b0dd9d38-c9da-4bb9-a626-d4b313aa7510?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
That strategy may ultimately make the relationship more stable.
But transitions from dependency to resilience can themselves create... friction. Especially when the more powerful partner exhibits a strategic and psychological tendency towards coercive control.

## Sovereignty is partly the ability to say no
Canada is doing what states have repeatedly done when dependence begins to feel dangerous.
**It is building exits.**
New customers. New ports. New pipelines. New alliances. New industries.
It can choose where it sells its oil. It can choose who buys its gas. It can decide how much refining capacity to build at home and which relationships to cultivate abroad. It can decide how much redundancy it is willing to pay for.
But the three layers of sovereignty remain stubbornly different.
* **Resource sovereignty:** we own it.
* **Market sovereignty:** we decide where it goes.
* **Corridor sovereignty:** we can actually get it there.

Venezuela demonstrates how financial architecture can constrain the second. Hormuz demonstrates vulnerability in the third. Panama shows what direct control of a corridor can mean. Suez shows how abruptly access, energy, finance and alliance hierarchy can intersect. Bab el-Mandeb shows that rerouting can simply move the vulnerability somewhere else. Malacca shows what happens when a major state recognizes the problem and spends decades trying to engineer around it.
Canada is now deliberately expanding its market sovereignty while discovering that **corridor sovereignty is harder**. It can choose where it sells its resources. It can choose how much independence it is willing to pay for. It cannot choose its geography, or its neighbor.
And somewhere between Burnaby and the open Pacific, in water close enough to feel like part of my own landscape, long-presumed neutral cooperation is fast becoming a real and serious question.
